title: Leveraging LLM-Based Agentic Systems to Generate Quantum Applications for Test Optimization
authors: Ming Tao, Yuechen Li, Tao Yue, Man Zhang, Aitor Arrieta Marcos
abstract: Quantum computing is increasingly explored for software engineering (SE) optimization, but translating natural-language (NL) task-level requirements into executable quantum applications still demands substantial quantum and programming expertise. We present QPipe, a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent architecture that autonomously turns NL requirements into traceable quantum-application workflows through specialized agents for requirement parsing, formulation, code generation, review, execution, and verification. We evaluate QPipe on 20 NL requirements, each associated with a real-world benchmark and a test-optimization problem. QPipe successfully completes the key stages of quantum-application generation across requirements, achieving average rates of 100% for code compilation and 96.7% for application execution and final-result combination, with average generation costs of 260.1 seconds and 1.89M tokens per requirement. Among the generated quantum applications that execute successfully, the returned solutions outperform the offline genetic algorithm baseline in most cases. Ablation results further show that QPipe's advantage depends on retaining code-generation skills, task knowledge, review feedback, and multi-agent decomposition. These results indicate that agentic coordination can support generation of executable quantum applications for tackling test optimization problems from real-world benchmarks.
summary: This paper introduces QPipe, an advanced LLM-based multi-agent system designed to automate the complex process of turning natural language requirements into working quantum applications for test optimization. By coordinating specialized agents—such as those handling encoding, code generation, and review—QPipe achieves high success rates in generating executable circuits that solve real-world problems better than classical benchmarks.
main_problem: The core problem is autonomously translating high-level, natural-language (NL) task requirements for Software Engineering optimization into fully executable quantum application workflows.
main_result: The proposed QPipe agentic system successfully generates executable quantum applications that solve test optimization problems, with generated solutions outperforming a classical genetic algorithm baseline in most tested cases.
method: A multi-agent LLM architecture (QPipe) is employed to guide the process through specialized agents responsible for parsing requirements, formulating QUBO/Ising models, generating code, reviewing logic, and executing the quantum workflow.
model_or_system: The system operates on quantum computing principles, encoding optimization problems into QUBO or Ising Hamiltonians ($\min x^	op Qx$). The execution targets ideal simulators using frameworks like Qiskit to run algorithms such as QAOA.
key_observables: Success rates for compilation (100%) and application execution (96.7%); solution quality measured by the QUBO-value reduction ratio (QRR) compared to a GA baseline; generation cost in seconds and tokens.
important_parameters: The system manages resource constraints like qubit budgets, often decomposing large problems into smaller, manageable subproblems for sequential processing.
main_assumptions: The evaluation assumes ideal quantum simulators are used, ignoring real-world noise or device constraints. The success relies on the stability of formulation patterns (QUBO/Ising) and LLM reasoning capabilities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the end-to-end workflow from NL input to executable output via specialized agents; pattern analysis shows successful runs consistently use QUBO formulations and QAOA algorithms, often decomposing problems into 4-6 subproblems.
paper_structure: The paper details the QPipe architecture, which involves sequential stages: requirement parsing $ightarrow$ quantum suitability analysis $ightarrow$ workflow planning/encoding $ightarrow$ code generation $ightarrow$ multi-agent review $ightarrow$ execution sandbox $ightarrow$ result combination and verification.
why_interesting: While focused on SE optimization rather than fundamental physics models, the reliance on QUBO/Ising formulations directly connects to quantum computational chemistry and materials science problems often modeled by Hamiltonians.
